prompt: An image whose Dockerfile has no `USER` line: which user does its container's process run as?

choices.text: Root, UID 0
choices.why: Right. And with no user namespace, that is the host's root.

choices.text: The user who ran `docker run`
choices.why: Ana's own UID would need `--user`; the default is the image's.

choices.text: `nobody`, for safety
choices.why: Docker picks nothing safer by itself.

choices.text: A random UID chosen at each start
choices.why: Docker does not randomise users; that is a choice some orchestrators make.

prompt: A runtime flaw lets a process get past a container's walls. Why does it matter whether that process was UID 0 or UID 65532?
hint: Which user does it arrive on the host as?

choices.text: It does not; a process past the walls is root anyway
choices.why: It arrives as the user it was; 65532 has no rights on the host.

choices.text: It arrives as that user: as root, that is the whole machine
choices.why: Right. As 65532, it is very little.

choices.text: UID 65532 processes cannot use the network
choices.why: They can; the difference is about the host's files and processes.

choices.text: Root processes run faster outside a container
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; power over the host is.

prompt: Which of these get worse when a container's process runs as root? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: What a bind-mounted host directory can be made to suffer
choices.why: Yes: root can rewrite anything in it.

choices.text: What a process past the walls can do on the host
choices.why: Yes: it lands there as root.

choices.text: How far a file-writing bug in the program reaches
choices.why: Yes: root can write anywhere in the container's filesystem.

choices.text: How long the image takes to pull
choices.why: The user has nothing to do with download size.

prompt: Why does the lesson write `USER 65532:65532` rather than `USER nonroot`, when both work?
hint: Who checks before starting the container?

choices.text: Names are slower to type
choices.why: Typing is not the argument.

choices.text: Names stop working after an image is pushed to a registry
choices.why: They keep working; they just cannot be verified without the image's `/etc/passwd`.

choices.text: Only a number lets an orchestrator verify it
choices.why: Right: orchestrators check non-root from a number; Kubernetes's `runAsNonRoot` refuses a name it cannot check.

choices.text: Distroless has no `nonroot` user
choices.why: It has one, as its `/etc/passwd` showed.

prompt: `shelf` running as UID 65532 listened on port 80 without trouble. Why?
hint: Read the value Ana printed from `/proc`.

choices.text: Port 80 is not a privileged port on Linux
choices.why: On the host it is reserved below 1024 by default; inside the container the setting differs.

choices.text: Distroless runs `shelf` as root despite `USER`
choices.why: `docker top` showed UID 65532.

choices.text: The port was published with `-p`
choices.why: No `-p` was given; the program bound the port inside.

choices.text: Docker sets `ip_unprivileged_port_start` to 0 in each container
choices.why: Right, so any user may bind any port in that namespace.

prompt: In the Alpine image, user 10001 could not create `/data/report.txt`. What fixed it?

choices.text: `chown app:app /data` before `USER`
choices.why: Right: hand over exactly the directory it writes to.

choices.text: Running the container with `--privileged`
choices.why: That would grant far more than one directory needs.

choices.text: Changing `USER` to a name instead of a number
choices.why: The name and number are the same user.

choices.text: Making `/data` a symbolic link to `/tmp`
choices.why: That avoids the question instead of answering it.

prompt: Distroless has no `cat`, yet Ana read `/etc/passwd` out of the running container with `docker ___ as-nonroot:/etc/passwd -`.
hint: The command that copies files between a container and the host.

prompt: `debian:trixie` is 187MB and `debian:trixie-slim` 119MB, both with 78 packages. What did slim remove?

choices.text: The shell and the package manager
choices.why: Both are still in slim; it has 259 programs in `/usr/bin`.

choices.text: Documentation, manual pages and locale files
choices.why: Right. The programs are all still there, shell and `apt` included.

choices.text: Half of the 78 packages, the ones nobody uses
choices.why: The count is identical: 78 in both.

choices.text: The C library
choices.why: Without it almost nothing in Debian would run.

prompt: `layers:two` creates a 50 MB file in one `RUN` and deletes it in the next. Why is its download 56.2MB?
hint: What does the second layer contain?

choices.text: The `rm` failed
choices.why: It ran; the file is gone from the container's view.

choices.text: Docker compresses deleted files badly
choices.why: Random bytes do not compress; but the point is that they are there at all.

choices.text: The first layer still holds the file; the second only hides it
choices.why: Right: a whiteout on top, the bytes underneath, downloaded on every pull.

choices.text: BuildKit caches the file in the image on purpose
choices.why: This is the layer model, not a cache.

prompt: `docker image ls layers` showed `layers:one` with what `CONTENT SIZE`, in MB?
Put the parts of a well-formed package install in the order they appear in one `RUN`.
hint: Lists first, clean-up last, all in one layer.

prompt: By the lesson's argument, why is a shell in a production image a cost even if the program never calls it?

choices.text: It slows the program down at start-up
choices.why: An unused shell costs nothing at run time.

choices.text: Shells are illegal in production images
choices.why: Nothing forbids them; the question is what they cost.

choices.text: It makes the image incompatible with Kubernetes
choices.why: Kubernetes runs images with shells all the time.

choices.text: A tool for intruders, a package to patch
choices.why: Right: one more of each. Surface is what is inside, not megabytes.

prompt: Match each practice to the problem it prevents.
hint: Five practices, five problems; one is a decoy.

pairs.right: Shipping the compiler and the sources

pairs.left: Install and clean up in one `RUN`
pairs.right: Deleted files kept in an earlier layer
A password copied into the image

right_distractors: A container that cannot reach the network

prompt: A colleague's Dockerfile ends `FROM debian:trixie-slim`, `COPY app /app`, `RUN chmod +x /app`, `CMD ["/app"]`. `app` is a static binary. Which single change removes the most surface?
hint: What does the program need from the base?

choices.text: Ship on distroless `static` instead
choices.why: Right: no shell, no package manager, and add the `USER` too.

choices.text: Switch to `debian:trixie`
choices.why: That adds 68MB of documentation and changes nothing else.

choices.text: Add `USER 65532:65532` and keep the base
choices.why: Worth doing, but the shell, `apt` and 259 programs stay.

choices.text: Delete `/usr/bin` in a later `RUN`
choices.why: The earlier layer keeps every file; the image does not shrink.
